Ugh, standing and delayed is a rough combo. A few questions so I can be useful: do you know roughly how late it's running, and is your main goal getting a seat, getting to class on time, or both?

I don't have live Tule Line data, so for real-time status check the transit agency's app or the station board. In general, commuter lines like this tend to have:
- Peak trains (around 6:30-8:30 a.m.) that fill up fast, especially at later stops
- Delays that cluster at rush hour, when one late train snowballs into the next
- Lighter loads on trains 15-20 minutes before the peak

If you can, tell me which trains are listed before and after yours and I can help you compare.
th train before is like 6:48ish i think. 20 min ride north, class starts at 9 mwf so i have slack. lowkey might just go earlier

With a 9 a.m. start and a 20-minute ride, you have a lot of slack, so an earlier train makes sense. Earlier trains are usually less crowded, so you'd likely get a seat, and a delay wouldn't threaten your class time.

To test it:
1. Try the earlier train for a week.
2. Note each day: departure time, seat or standing, minutes late, arrival time.
3. Compare against your current train.

If the earlier one is consistently calmer, switch. Just confirm the timetable first, since I'm not sure of those exact times.
ok. also i have a $54 student monthly pass, is it even worth keeping

Quick math: a monthly pass is worth it if it costs less than your single fares added up. At $54 a month, you break even at the number of rides where single fares total $54.

For example, if a one-way fare is $X, you need about 54 / X rides a month. Commuting every weekday is roughly 40 rides in a month (20 days x 2), so the pass is almost certainly worth it unless single fares are very cheap. If you're riding only 2-3 days a week, it's closer. What does a single one-way fare cost? I can run the exact number.

Also check whether the pass covers other trips, like weekends, since that adds value.
